claim: Mechanical force is critical for the interaction between an αβ T cell receptor (TCR) and a peptide-bound major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecule to initiate productive T-cell activation.
source: Mechanical force is critical for the interaction between an αβ T cell receptor (TCR) and a peptide-bound major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecule to initiate productive T-cell activation.
evidence: This is a statement of established understanding in the field, supported by the broader context of the manuscript and citations throughout.

claim: TCR α and β chains move asymmetrically under load, which impacts the interface with pMHC, in particular the peptide-sensing CDR3 loops.
source: We found that TCR α and β chains move asymmetrically, which impacts the interface with pMHC, in particular the peptide-sensing CDR3 loops.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MD simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: For the wild-type agonist, the complex stabilizes in a load-dependent manner while antagonists destabilize it.
source: For the wild-type agonist, the complex stabilizes in a load-dependent manner while antagonists destabilize it.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations, supported by contact analysis and occupancy data in Figures 3, 6, and 8.

claim: Simulations of the Cβ FG-loop deletion reduce the catch bond response.
source: Simulations of the Cβ FG-loop deletion, which reduces the catch bond response, and simulations with in silico mutant peptides further support the observed behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data presented in Appendix 1 and referenced in the main text.

claim: The combined role of interdomain motion, fluctuating forces, and interfacial contacts determines the mechanical response and fine peptide discrimination by a TCR.
source: The present results highlight the combined role of interdomain motion, fluctuating forces, and interfacial contacts in determining the mechanical response and fine peptide discrimination by a TCR, thereby resolving the conundrum of nearly identical crystal structures of TCRαβ-pMHC agonist and antagonist complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective simulation results and analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The αβ TCR consists of the heterodimeric receptor TCRαβ formed by α and β chains each containing the pMHC-binding variable (V) and constant (C) domains.
source: The αβ TCR (αβTCR) consists of the heterodimeric receptor TCRαβ formed by α and β chains each containing the pMHC-binding variable (V) and constant (C) domains (Figure 1 and Figure 2A), and the noncovalently associated cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3) subunits that have cytoplasmic tails containing motifs for downstream signaling (Rudolph et al., 2006; Wang and Reinherz, 2012; Brazin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR structure, supported by citations and illustrated in figures.

claim: The TCR recognizes its cognate pMHC on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell (APC) at low or even single copy numbers from a pool of about 10^5 different self-pMHC molecules.
source: The TCR recognizes its cognate pMHC on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell (APC) at low or even single copy numbers from a pool of about 105 different self-pMHC molecules (Sykulev et al., 1996; Brameshuber et al., 2018), while it also exhibits reactivity with certain closely related peptide variants, with similar or strikingly altered functional T-cell responses (Ding et al., 1999; Hausmann et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2004; Borbulevych et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2012; Birnbaum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: TCRαβ-pMHC equilibrium binding affinity is in the μM to hundreds of μM range.
source: Considering the μM to hundreds of μM TCRαβ-pMHC equilibrium binding affinity (Wang and Reinherz, 2012), several models have been proposed to account for the exquisite specificity and sensitivity of the αβTCR (Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Brazin et al., 2015; Schamel et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2019; Mariuzza et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A cognate peptide antigen elicits a catch bond behavior where the TCRαβ-pMHC bond lifetime increases with force that peaks in the 10–20 pN range.
source: A cognate peptide antigen elicits a catch bond behavior where the TCRαβ-pMHC bond lifetime increases with force that peaks in the 10–20 pN range, and is observed with the clonotypic ligand-binding TCRαβ heterodimer in isolation or with the holoreceptor αβTCR including the non-covalently associated CD3 signaling subunit dimers (CD3ϵγ, CD3ϵδ, and CD3ζζ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: The catch bond is coupled with a roughly 10 nm structural transition in both TCRαβ heterodimer and holoreceptor αβTCR.
source: The catch bond is coupled with a roughly 10 nm structural transition in both (Das et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016; Banik et al., 2021), which supports the notion that the αβTCR acts as a mechanosensor (Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Brazin et al., 2015; Brazin et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2023; Reinherz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The αβTCR acts as a mechanosensor.
source: The catch bond is coupled with a roughly 10 nm structural transition in both (Das et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016; Banik et al., 2021), which supports the notion that the αβTCR acts as a mechanosensor (Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Brazin et al., 2015; Brazin et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2023; Reinherz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by multiple cited studies and the structural transition data.

claim: In a previous MD study, applying a 16-pN force to the JM22 TCR-pMHC complex suppressed domain motion and enhanced the fit among domains.
source: In our previous molecular dynamics (MD) study (Hwang et al., 2020), instead of enforcing dissociation of the complex with high force, as done in steered MD simulations (Sibener et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019), we applied pN-level forces and examined the behavior of the JM22 TCR complexed with an HLA-A*02:01 molecule presenting a peptide from an influenza virus matrix protein. We found that the TCRαβ-pMHC complex is in a loosely-bound state in the absence of load, which allows domain motion. Application of a 16-pN force suppresses the motion and overall enhances the fit among domains.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, cited and described.

claim: The TCRαβ-pMHC catch bond arises due to stabilization of the interface by altering the conformational motion of TCRαβ.
source: We proposed a model where the TCRαβ-pMHC catch bond arises due to stabilization of the interface by altering the conformational motion of TCRαβ.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on previous simulation results.

claim: The A6 TCR recognizes the Tax peptide (LLFGYPVYV) of the human T lymphotropic virus type 1 bound to HLA-A*02:01.
source: To this end, we study the A6 TCR, which recognizes the Tax peptide (LLFGYPVYV) of the human T lymphotropic virus type 1 (Garboczi et al., 1996b) bound to HLA-A*02:01, the same MHC as for JM22.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the A6 TCR system, supported by citation.

claim: All-atom MD simulations were performed with the Tax peptide (wild type; WT) and four mutant peptides with a single-residue substitution: Y5F, V7R, P6A, and Y8A.
source: We perform all-atom MD simulations with the Tax peptide (wild type; WT) (Garboczi et al., 1996a) and four mutant peptides with a single-residue substitution: Y5F (Scott et al., 2011), V7R, P6A, and Y8A (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the simulation systems studied, with citations to the structural sources.

claim: The crystallographic structures of the WT and mutant peptide complexes are very similar.
source: While the crystallographic structures of these complexes are very similar (Ding et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2011; Figure 2C), they differ in immunogenicity.
evidence: This is supported by citation and visual comparison in Figure 2C.

claim: P6A and Y8A are weak antagonists because they inhibit T-cell function only at 1000-times higher molar concentration than that needed by the WT for activation.
source: P6A and Y8A are weak antagonists because they inhibit T-cell function only at 1000-times higher molar concentration than that needed by the WT for activation (Hausmann et al., 1999; Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claim: Y5F is similar to WT in terms of equilibrium binding affinity and T-cell activation in vitro.
source: Y5F is similar to WT in terms of equilibrium binding affinity and T-cell activation in vitro (Hausmann et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claim: V7R induces effector functions comparable to WT at 10- to 100-times higher concentrations.
source: V7R induces effector functions comparable to WT at 10- to 100-times higher concentrations (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claim: To simulate a complex under load, the distance between the terminal Cα atoms of the complex was held at a set extension for the duration of the simulation.
source: To simulate a complex under load, we held the distance between the terminal Cα atoms of the complex (Figure 2A) at a set extension for the duration of the simulation.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology used.

claim: Harmonic positional restraints were applied to the terminal Cα atoms so that they were allowed to fluctuate in position, resulting in instantaneous fluctuation in the applied force.
source: This was done by applying harmonic positional restraints so that the terminal Cα atoms were allowed to fluctuate in position, hence resulting in instantaneous fluctuation in the applied force akin to loading in experiments.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: Simulations were referred to as either low or high load based on the average load, which was around the physiological 10–20 pN range.
source: We refer to a simulation as either low or high load based on the average load, which was around the physiological 10–20 pN range (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the classification scheme for simulations, with data in Table 1.

claim: Differences between the WT and peptide mutants lie in dynamic responses to applied load.
source: We found that differences between the WT and peptide mutants lie in dynamic responses to applied load.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations.

claim: In the WT, physiological level load stabilized the TCRαβ-pMHC interface as well as the subdomain motion within TCRαβ.
source: In the WT, physiological level load stabilized the TCRαβ-pMHC interface as well as the subdomain motion within TCRαβ.
evidence: This is a finding from the WT simulations, supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claim: Modified agonists maintained stable contacts, yet high loads led to destabilization.
source: Modified agonists maintained stable contacts, yet high loads led to destabilization.
evidence: This is a finding from the modified agonist simulations, supported by data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Antagonists had less stable interfaces under load as the mutated residues disrupted surrounding interfacial contacts.
source: Antagonists had less stable interfaces under load as the mutated residues disrupted surrounding interfacial contacts.
evidence: This is a finding from the antagonist simulations, supported by data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Motion within the TCR, such as the Vα-Vβ scissoring and an asymmetric bending of the V-module relative to the C-module, were coupled to the interactions between the variable domains and pMHC.
source: Motion within the TCR, such as the Vα-Vβ scissoring as observed in Hwang et al., 2020, and an asymmetric bending of the V-module relative to the C-module, were coupled to the interactions between the variable domains and pMHC such that a single-residue mutation in the peptide affected the conformational behavior of the whole TCR.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, supported by data in Figures 4-7.

claim: A single-residue mutation in the peptide affected the conformational behavior of the whole TCR.
source: Motion within the TCR, such as the Vα-Vβ scissoring as observed in Hwang et al., 2020, and an asymmetric bending of the V-module relative to the C-module, were coupled to the interactions between the variable domains and pMHC such that a single-residue mutation in the peptide affected the conformational behavior of the whole TCR.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations comparing WT and mutants.

claim: The conserved TCRαβ framework motion is leveraged when determining the mechanically matched pMHC, a mechanism that is broadly applicable to different TCRαβ systems.
source: The present results suggest that the conserved TCRαβ framework motion is leveraged when determining the mechanically matched pMHC, a mechanism that is broadly applicable to different TCRαβ systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results and comparison with previous work.

claim: WTlow had the least number of high-occupancy contacts with pMHC, followed by WT0 and WThigh.
source: WTlow had the least number of contacts, followed by WT0 and WThigh, indicating low and high loads may have opposite effect on the interfacial stability.
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 3A.

claim: Vαβ-pMHC without the C-module formed the most contacts with pMHC.
source: Vαβ-pMHC without the C-module formed the most contacts.
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 3A.

claim: Without a proper load, the C-module is detrimental to the stability of the interface with pMHC.
source: This indicates that without a proper load, the C-module is detrimental to the stability of the interface with pMHC, as we found previously for the JM22 TCR (Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference from the contact data, supported by previous findings.

claim: In WThigh and Vαβ-pMHC, high-occupancy contacts form more compact clusters.
source: In WThigh and Vαβ-pMHC, high-occupancy contacts form more compact clusters.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial distribution of contacts shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The trend in buried surface area (BSA) of TCRαβ residues involved in high-occupancy contacts follows the same trend as the number of high occupancy contacts.
source: Exposure to water of the TCRαβ residues involved in those contacts was measured by their buried surface area (BSA), which follows the same trend as the number of high occupancy contacts (Figure 3A vs. Figure 3G)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Figure 3A and 3G.

claim: The trend in BSA also applied to the root-mean square fluctuation (RMSF) of Tax peptide backbone Cα atoms.
source: Furthermore, this trend also applied to the root-mean square fluctuation (RMSF) of Tax peptide backbone Cα atoms, even though RMSF values were small (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by the RMSF data in Figure 3H.

claim: The WT complex has a relatively strong affinity as a TCRαβ (about 1 μM).
source: Experimentally, the WT complex has a relatively strong affinity as a TCRαβ (about 1 μM) (Ding et al., 1999), which may be why the interface with pMHC involved more contacts in WT0 compared to WTlow.
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claim: At low load, the short distance between restraints allows wider transverse motion that generates a shear stress or a bending moment at the interface.
source: At low load, the short distance between restraints on the ends of the complex (Figure 2A) allows wider transverse motion that in turn generates a shear stress or a bending moment at the interface.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation setup and observed dynamics.

claim: Transverse stress will be less for WT0 where the end moves freely, and for WThigh where lateral motion is suppressed.
source: Transverse stress will be less for WT0 where the end moves freely, and for WThigh where lateral motion is suppressed.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation conditions.

claim: The RMSF of the center of mass of the Cα atoms of the peptide in the transverse direction was 16.3 Å for WTlow and 12.7 Å for WThigh.
source: The extent of transverse motion can be seen by the RMSF of the center of mass of the Cα atoms of the peptide in the transverse direction, which was 16.3 Å for WTlow and 12.7 Å for WThigh.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the simulations.

claim: The high stability of Vαβ-pMHC and WThigh agree well with the results for JM22.
source: The high stability of Vαβ-pMHC and WThigh agree well with the results for JM22 (Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous simulation results.

claim: The number of high-occupancy Vα-Vβ contacts increased slightly in Vαβ-pMHC compared to the unliganded systems.
source: Compared to the unliganded systems (Vαβ and Tαβ; Table 2), the number of high-occupancy Vα-Vβ contacts increased slightly in Vαβ-pMHC ('V' in Figure 4A), while it decreased in full TCRαβ-pMHC complexes ('0', 'Low', and 'High' in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 4A.

claim: The number of high-occupancy Vα-Vβ contacts decreased in full TCRαβ-pMHC complexes compared to unliganded systems.
source: Compared to the unliganded systems (Vαβ and Tαβ; Table 2), the number of high-occupancy Vα-Vβ contacts increased slightly in Vαβ-pMHC ('V' in Figure 4A), while it decreased in full TCRαβ-pMHC complexes ('0', 'Low', and 'High' in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 4A.

claim: The Vα-Vβ interface is difficult to organize with the restrictions imposed by the bound pMHC, except in the absence of the constant domains.
source: This shows that the Vα-Vβ interface is difficult to organize with the restrictions imposed by the bound pMHC, except in the absence of the constant domains.
evidence: This is an inference from the contact count data.

claim: The number of Vα-Vβ contacts in the liganded systems is the smallest for WTlow.
source: The number of Vα-Vβ contacts in the liganded systems is the smallest for WTlow, similar to the case for the number of contacts with pMHC (Figure 3A), again reflecting a destabilizing effect with low load.
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 4A.

claim: The amplitude of PC1 is lower when the number of Vα-Vβ contacts is higher.
source: The amplitude of PC1 is lower when the number of Vα-Vβ contacts is higher (Figure 4A vs. Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Among triad systems with bound pMHC, WTlow differed significantly in the PC1 direction compared to others.
source: Among triad systems with bound pMHC, WTlow differed significantly in the PC1 direction compared to others (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, darker colors).
evidence: This is supported by the dot product analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Unliganded Tαβ and Vαβ had greater fluctuation in the CDR3 distance.
source: Unliganded Tαβ and Vαβ had greater fluctuation in the CDR3 distance (larger std), as they are unrestrained by pMHC.
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Among the pMHC-bound systems, WThigh and Vαβ-pMHC had small CDR3 distance (averages of 10.3 and 10.5 Å, respectively).
source: Among the pMHC-bound systems, WThigh and Vαβ-pMHC had small CDR3 distance (averages of 10.3 and 10.5 Å, respectively; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B C).
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: CDR3 distance was larger for WT0 (11.3 Å), which reflects an altered interface with pMHC.
source: CDR3 distance was larger for WT0 (11.3 Å), which reflects an altered interface with pMHC.
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance data and is an inference about the interface.

claim: For WTlow, the CDR3 distance varied more widely, with more than a 2-fold increase in standard deviation.
source: For WTlow, the CDR3 distance varied more widely, with more than a 2-fold increase in standard deviation.
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: No clear correlation could be seen between individual PC modes and the CDR3 distance.
source: If any of the PC modes is strongly correlated with the CDR3 distance, the corresponding histogram would exhibit a slanted profile. However, no clear correlation could be seen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the changes in CDR3 distance may depend on combinations of PCs.
evidence: This is supported by the 2D histograms in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The changes in CDR3 distance may depend on combinations of PCs.
source: However, no clear correlation could be seen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the changes in CDR3 distance may depend on combinations of PCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation with individual PCs.

claim: The CDR3 distance varies with the triad arm angles.
source: Histograms of the three angles (Figure 4C) show a clearer difference than individual PCs among the systems tested, and the CDR3 distance varies with the angles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the angle histograms and CDR3 distance vs. angle plots in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The CDR3 motion is coupled to the Vα-Vβ motion, especially the scissoring motion.
source: These results show that the CDR3 motion is coupled to the Vα-Vβ motion, especially the scissoring motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of triad angles and CDR3 distance.

claim: The number of high-occupancy Cα-Cβ contacts did not vary significantly (in the 31–34 range) and they were more than the number of Vα-Vβ contacts.
source: The number of high-occupancy Cα-Cβ contacts did not vary significantly (in the 31–34 range) and they were more than the number of Vα-Vβ contacts, similar to the case for the JM22 TCR (Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the contact analysis, compared with previous work.

claim: The C-module influences the V-module as a single unit.
source: The C-module thereby influences the V-module as a single unit.
evidence: This is an inference from the contact data showing the C-module moves as a unit.

claim: PC1 (V-C bend) was similar among systems, as seen by the values of dot products being close to 1.0.
source: PC1 (V-C bend; Figure 5A) was similar among systems, as seen by the values of dot products being close to 1.0 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the dot product analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Vα bends more compared to Vβ, as can be gleaned from the longer PC arrows for Vα.
source: We noticed that Vα bends more compared to Vβ, as can be gleaned from the longer PC arrows for Vα (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the visual representation in Figure 5A.

claim: Binding of pMHC increases the α-chain motion compared to Tαβ, which is the greatest in WTlow.
source: Compared to Tαβ, binding of pMHC increases the α-chain motion, which is the greatest in WTlow (Figure 5C, PC1 in top row).
evidence: This is supported by the amplitude difference data in Figure 5C.

claim: The greater degree of Vα-Cα motion is consistent with the smaller number of Vα-Cα contacts compared to Vβ-Cβ.
source: The greater degree of Vα-Cα motion is consistent with the smaller number of Vα-Cα contacts compared to Vβ-Cβ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distributions of ∠TCRα varied more compared to ∠TCRβ.
source: Distributions of ∠TCRα varied more compared to ∠TCRβ (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the hinge angle histograms in Figure 5D.

claim: For WTlow and WThigh, CDR3 distance decreases with increasing hinge angles, especially with ∠TCRα.
source: For WTlow and WThigh, CDR3 distance decreases with increasing hinge angles, especially with ∠TCRα (Figure 5E), which suggests that unbending of the V-module under load helps with bringing the CDR3 loops closer together.
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance vs. hinge angle plots in Figure 5E.

claim: Unbending of the V-module under load helps with bringing the CDR3 loops closer together.
source: For WTlow and WThigh, CDR3 distance decreases with increasing hinge angles, especially with ∠TCRα (Figure 5E), which suggests that unbending of the V-module under load helps with bringing the CDR3 loops closer together.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between hinge angles and CDR3 distance.

claim: The asymmetric response of the whole TCRαβ to load affects the binding with pMHC by controlling the relative positioning between the CDR3 loops via the Vα-Vβ motion.
source: These results suggest a mechanism by which the asymmetric response of the whole TCRαβ to load affects the binding with pMHC by controlling the relative positioning between the CDR3 loops via the Vα-Vβ motion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the V-C and Vα-Vβ motion analyses.

claim: The Cβ FG-loop plays a critical role in the asymmetric V-C motion mechanism.
source: For this, the Cβ FG-loop plays a critical role, as simulations of the bound complex without the Cβ FG-loop resulted in a smaller ∠TCRβ and an over-extended ∠TCRα (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by the dFG simulation results in Appendix 1.

claim: In the WT crystal structure, the side chain of Y5 in the Tax peptide is located between the CDR3 loops of Vα and Vβ while V7 mainly contacts CDR3β.
source: In the WT crystal structure, the side chain of Y5 in the Tax peptide is located between the CDR3 loops of Vα and Vβ while V7 mainly contacts CDR3β (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is structural information from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P6 makes one contact with CDR3β.
source: P6 makes one contact with CDR3β.
evidence: This is structural information from the crystal structure.

claim: The side chain of Y8 is located between CDR3β and the α1 helix of MHC.
source: The side chain of Y8 is located between CDR3β and the α1 helix of MHC.
evidence: This is structural information from the crystal structure.

claim: Crystal structures of point mutants of Y5, V7, P6, and Y8 are very similar in terms of interfacial contacts, docking angle, and CDR loop conformations, with the only structurally observable difference located at CDR3β.
source: Crystal structures of point mutants of these four residues are very similar in terms of interfacial contacts, docking angle, and CDR loop conformations, with the only structurally observable difference located at CDR3β (Figure 2B and C; Ding et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and visual comparison in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Point mutations profoundly affect dynamics of the complex.
source: However, point mutations profoundly affect dynamics of the complex, as explained below.
evidence: This is a summary statement introducing the results for mutant systems.

claim: Modified agonists Y5F and V7R had about the same number of contacts with pMHC as the WT complexes, but high load resulted in fewer contacts.
source: Modified agonists Y5F and V7R had about the same number of contacts with pMHC as the WT complexes, but high load resulted in fewer contacts, indicating a potential slip bond behavior (Figure 6A), although loss of contacts in Y5Fhigh might have been due to a higher load experienced compared to other complexes at the same extension (23.7 pN; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 6A and Table 1.

claim: Antagonists P6A and Y8A had overall fewer contacts with pMHC without a consistent load dependence.
source: Antagonists P6A and Y8A had overall fewer contacts with pMHC without a consistent load dependence (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 6A.

claim: In Y5F, the hydrogen bond with αS31 cannot form, and many of the nonpolar contacts with F5 break under load later during the simulation.
source: In Y5F, the hydrogen bond with αS31 cannot form, and many of the nonpolar contacts with F5 break under load later during the simulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the contact heat maps in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Y5-αS31 hydrogen bond may stabilize the interface with pMHC by arranging other nearby residues to form nonpolar contacts in favorable positions.
source: Thus, the Y5-αS31 hydrogen bond may stabilize the interface with pMHC by arranging other nearby residues to form nonpolar contacts in favorable positions; its absence would make the nonpolar contacts more prone to break under load.
evidence: This is an inference from the contact dynamics observed in Y5F simulations.

claim: Y5F has kinetic and cytotoxicity profiles similar to WT experimentally.
source: Experimentally, Y5F has kinetic and cytotoxicity profiles similar to WT (Hausmann et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claim: In V7R, nonpolar contacts with CDR3β form with reduced occupancy, and contacts involving Y8 are also disrupted.
source: On the other hand, V7 of the WT peptide forms nonpolar contacts with residues in CDR3β (Figure 3C–E, Figure 6C). In V7R, nonpolar contacts with CDR3β form with reduced occupancy, and contacts involving Y8 are also disrupted (Figure 6C vs. Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the contact heat maps in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: For antagonists, more contacts broke, which involve non-mutated residues such as Y5 and V7.
source: For antagonists, more contacts broke, which again involve non-mutated residues such as Y5 and V7 (Figure 6D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the contact heat maps in Figure 6D-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Binding of the A6 TCR to pMHC containing the P6A or Y8A peptide was not detected in vitro experimentally.
source: Experimentally, binding of the A6 TCR to pMHC containing the P6A or Y8A peptide was not detected in vitro (Ding et al., 1999).
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claim: Y8A could exhibit a catch bond in principle, but forming the complex in the loaded state may be kinetically inaccessible.
source: Thus, Y8A in principle could exhibit a catch bond, but forming the complex in the loaded state may be kinetically inaccessible.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results and experimental data.

claim: The modified agonists had more Vα-Vβ contacts than WThigh while the antagonists had fewer, except for Y8Ahigh.
source: The modified agonists had more Vα-Vβ contacts than WThigh while the antagonists had fewer, except for Y8Ahigh (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Point mutations to the peptide cause alterations in the load-dependence of the interface and the Vα-Vβ motion.
source: These results suggest that point mutations to the peptide cause alterations in the load-dependence of the interface and the Vα-Vβ motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of mutant systems.

claim: The mutants affected the average V-C BOC similarly as that for dFGhigh.
source: The mutants affected the average V-C BOC similarly as that for dFGhigh (Figure 7C and D vs. Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the BOC representations in Figure 7C-D and Appendix 1—figure 1C.

claim: Among the mutants, Y8Ahigh had an average BOC approaching that of WThigh.
source: Among them, Y8Ahigh had an average BOC approaching that of WThigh, which aligns with the comparable number of contacts with pMHC (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the BOC representation in Figure 7D and contact data in Figure 6A.

claim: Displacements of centroids from the corresponding ones in WThigh were overall greater for the α chain than the β chain in mutants.
source: To quantify deformation of the average BOC, we measured displacements of centroids from the corresponding ones in WThigh, which were overall greater for the α chain than the β chain (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A B).
evidence: This is supported by the displacement data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: The mutants had fewer Vα-Cα contacts than WThigh and a similar number of Vβ-Cβ contacts.
source: Consistent with this, the mutants had fewer Vα-Cα contacts than WThigh and a similar number of Vβ-Cβ contacts (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: This is supported by the contact count data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: The greater motion of the α chain than the β chain was observed in the mutant systems.
source: Similar to the WT systems, the greater motion of the α chain than the β chain was observed in the mutant systems, as seen from the differences in V-C PC1 amplitudes (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A B).
evidence: This is supported by the amplitude difference data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Dot products of the BOC PC1 between WT and mutants revealed that the direction of motion differed by varying degrees, which was more for V7Rhigh and Y8A.
source: However, dot products of the BOC PC1 between WT and mutants revealed that the direction of motion differed by varying degrees, which was more for V7Rhigh and Y8A (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C vs. Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the dot product analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Point mutations on the WT peptide can affect the conformational motion of the whole TCRαβ, in addition to the average BOC.
source: Thus, point mutations on the WT peptide can affect the conformational motion of the whole TCRαβ, in addition to the average BOC.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the BOC and PC analysis of mutant systems.

claim: In silico antagonists did exhibit reduction in contacts with pMHC.
source: The in silico antagonists did exhibit reduction in contacts with pMHC while the results were mixed for the in silico WT, especially for A8Y where the introduced tyrosine is bulkier than the original alanine.
evidence: This is supported by the in silico mutation simulation results in Appendix 2.

claim: For the intramolecular contacts, the Cα-Cβ interface contacts were excluded from the total occupancy calculation since they are larger in number and did not differ significantly across different systems.
source: For the intramolecular contacts, we excluded the Cα-Cβ interface contacts since they are larger in number compared to other interfaces and did not differ significantly across different systems.
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained in the context of the analysis.

claim: The C-module moves mostly as a single unit.
source: Thus, the C-module moves mostly as a single unit (Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the contact data and previous work.

claim: For WT0, the intermolecular contact occupancy stayed at around 20 and for WTlow, it decreased later in simulation.
source: For WT0, the intermolecular contact occupancy stayed at around 20 (WT in Figure 8A, horizontal bar on the bottom) and for WTlow, it decreased later in simulation (WT in Figure 8A, darkening of circles without outline).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A.

claim: The intramolecular contact occupancy remained relatively constant for both WT0 and WTlow.
source: In comparison, the intramolecular contact occupancy remained relatively constant for both WT0 and WTlow (WT in Figure 8B, horizontal bar on the bottom and circles without outline).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8B.

claim: For WThigh, the intermolecular contact occupancy was steady and the intramolecular occupancy remained high, indicating the subdomains are held together tightly.
source: For WThigh, the intermolecular contact occupancy was steady even with wider fluctuation in force (WT in Figure 8A, outlined circles), and the intramolecular occupancy also remained high, indicating the subdomains are held together tightly (WT in Figure 8B, outlined circles).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: For dFGlow, the intermolecular contact occupancy stayed low and intramolecular occupancy was relatively constant.
source: For dFGlow, the intermolecular contact occupancy stayed low and intramolecular occupancy was relatively constant (dFG in Figure 8A and B, circles without outline).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: In dFGhigh, the contact occupancy with pMHC increased, but the intramolecular contact occupancy became low, suggesting that the complex is not as tightly coupled compared to WT.
source: In dFGhigh, the contact occupancy with pMHC increased (dFG in Figure 8A, outlined circles), but the intramolecular contact occupancy became low (dFG in Figure 8B, outlined circles), which suggests that the complex is not as tightly coupled compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A-B and is an inference about coupling.

claim: For modified agonists, the no load and low load cases had overall higher occupancy, both with pMHC and within TCRαβ, but occupancy fluctuated more.
source: For modified agonists, the no load and low load cases had overall higher occupancy, both with pMHC and within TCRαβ, but occupancy fluctuated more as can be seen by the changes in colors in the occupancy trajectories (Y5F and V7R in Figure 8A and B, horizontal bars on the bottom and circles without outlines).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Under high load, intermolecular contact occupancy decreased over time for modified agonists.
source: Under high load, intermolecular contact occupancy decreased over time (Y5F and V7R in Figure 8A, darkening of outlined circles) while intramolecular contact occupancy either increased (Y5Fhigh) or decreased (V7Rhigh) relative to the respective low load cases.
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A.

claim: For antagonists, both occupancy measures were lower than the WT, and further reduction could be seen over time in some cases.
source: For antagonists, both occupancy measures were lower than the WT, and further reduction could be seen over time in some cases (P6A and Y8A in Figure 8A and B, darkening of colors in outlined circles).
evidence: This is supported by the time-dependent occupancy data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: For WT, the peptide angle fluctuated more for WTlow than WThigh.
source: For WT, the peptide angle fluctuated more for WTlow than WThigh (WT in Figure 8C) where 58.4°±3.6° (avg±std after 500 ns) for WThigh reflects a diagonal binding.
evidence: This is supported by the peptide angle trajectories in Figure 8C.

claim: For dFGlow, the peptide changed orientation by more than 20°, and for dFGhigh, it stabilized, but at a higher value than WThigh, suggesting a more orthogonal binding.
source: For dFGlow, the peptide changed orientation by more than 20°, and for dFGhigh, it stabilized, but at a higher value than WThigh, which also was reached in dFGlow later during simulation, suggesting a more orthogonal binding (dFG in Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by the peptide angle trajectories in Figure 8C and is an inference about binding geometry.

claim: For modified agonists, the peptide angle was affected more under high loads, becoming more orthogonal compared to WThigh.
source: For modified agonists, similar to the behaviors of the total intra- and intermolecular contact occupancy, the peptide angle was affected more under high loads, again becoming more orthogonal compared to WThigh (Y5F and V7R in Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by the peptide angle trajectories in Figure 8C.

claim: For antagonists, the angle overall fluctuated more under no load or settled to different values under high load.
source: For antagonists, the angle overall fluctuated more under no load or settled to different values under high load.
evidence: This is supported by the peptide angle trajectories in Figure 8C.

claim: TCRαβ activates the catch bond via altering its conformational dynamics instead of using defined conformational changes as seen in other catch bond systems.
source: Instead of using defined conformational changes as seen in other catch bond systems, TCRαβ activates the catch bond via altering its conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: A main feature of the TCRαβ framework is the smaller number of contacts for the Vα-Cα compared to the Vβ-Cβ interface.
source: A main feature of the TCRαβ framework is the smaller number of contacts for the Vα-Cα compared to the Vβ-Cβ interface.
evidence: This is a finding from the contact analysis.

claim: The smaller number of Vα-Cα contacts causes an asymmetric V-C motion, primarily bending, where Vα moves more compared to Vβ relative to the C-module.
source: This causes an asymmetric V-C motion, primarily bending, where Vα moves more compared to Vβ relative to the C-module, which serves as a base.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the V-C motion analysis.

claim: The asymmetric V-C motion generates relative motion between Vα and Vβ, which can destabilize the contacts with pMHC, especially by affecting the distance between CDR3 loops.
source: This in turn generates relative motion between Vα and Vβ, which can destabilize the contacts with pMHC, especially by affecting the distance between CDR3 loops that play the most direct role for sensing the bound peptide (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion illustrated in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Applying a physiological level force stabilizes the interface by straining the whole complex into a more tightly coupled state.
source: Applying a physiological level force stabilizes the interface by straining the whole complex into a more tightly coupled state, as can be seen by the increase of both inter- and intramolecular contacts in WThigh (Figures 8 and 9C).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion supported by data in Figures 8 and 9C.

claim: The CDR3 distance of WThigh (10.3±0.3 Å) was shorter than that of WT0 or WTlow and also shorter than the 10.9 Å CDR3 distance in the crystal structure (PDB 1AO7).
source: The CDR3 distance of WThigh (10.3±0.3 Å; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) was shorter than that of WT0 or WTlow (Figure 4D), and it is also shorter than the 10.9 Å CDR3 distance in the crystal structure (PDB 1AO7).
evidence: This is supported by the CDR3 distance data and comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: The applied load slightly increases the spacing between pMHC and TCRαβ, which provides room for the CDR3 loops to adjust and allow other contacts to 'lock' into more stable states.
source: The applied load slightly increases the spacing between pMHC and TCRαβ, which provides room for the CDR3 loops to adjust as well as allow other contacts to 'lock' into more stable states with higher and more persistent occupancy.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results about the mechanism of stabilization.

claim: Absence of load or low load do not properly channel the framework motion and thereby increase exposure to water and destabilize the interface.
source: Absence of load or low load do not properly channel the framework motion and thereby increase exposure to water (Figure 3F and G) and destabilize the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the BSA and contact stability data.

claim: The Cβ FG-loop stabilizes the Vβ-Cβ interface, thereby contributing to the asymmetric V-C motion.
source: The Cβ FG-loop stabilizes the Vβ-Cβ interface, thereby contributing to the asymmetric V-C motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dFG simulation results.

claim: The Cβ FG-loop controls the relative orientation between Vβ and Cβ, hence it affects the orientation of the CDR loops of the V-module with respect to the loading direction.
source: It also controls the relative orientation between Vβ and Cβ, hence it affects the orientation of the CDR loops of the V-module with respect to the loading direction (Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dFG simulation results shown in Appendix 1.

claim: The behaviors of the dFG mutant are consistent with the reduced catch bond response observed experimentally.
source: The behaviors of the dFG mutant are consistent with the reduced catch bond response observed experimentally (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of simulation results with experimental data.

claim: Consistency in findings between the present study and previous simulations using JM22 TCR underscores that the proposed mechanism based on the asymmetric framework motion is applicable to other TCRαβ systems.
source: Consistency in these findings between the present study and our previous simulations using JM22 TCR (Hwang et al., 2020) also underscores that the proposed mechanism based on the asymmetric framework motion is applicable to other TCRαβ systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing results across different TCR systems.

claim: The Vγδ-Cαβ chimera forms a catch bond with its sulfatide ligand-loaded CD1d molecule, providing additional experimental support for the proposed mechanism.
source: Furthermore, while the γδ TCR involved in transitional immunity operates as a slip-bond receptor, the Vγδ-Cαβ chimera forms a catch bond with its sulfatide ligand-loaded CD1d molecule (Mallis et al., 2021), which provides additional experimental support for the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study that supports the proposed mechanism.

claim: In the absence of bond dissociation events within the microsecond-long simulation, the catch bond manifests as stabilization of high-occupancy contacts and interfacial fit under load.
source: In the absence of bond dissociation events within the microsecond-long simulation, the catch bond manifests as stabilization of high-occupancy contacts and interfacial fit under load.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how catch bond behavior is observed in the simulations.

claim: Slip bond will exhibit destabilization of the interface under load, as seen for antagonists.
source: Conversely, slip bond will exhibit destabilization of the interface under load, as seen for antagonists (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the antagonist simulation results.

claim: Atomistic simulations can be used to design mutant TCRs possessing altered load dependence.
source: In addition to agreeing with previous experiments mentioned above, our atomistic simulations can be used to design mutant TCRs possessing altered load dependence.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the simulation approach.

claim: After engagement with a cognate pMHC under load, reversible transition to an extended state is possible.
source: After engagement with a cognate pMHC under load, reversible transition to an extended state is possible. This has been observed both during in vitro single-molecule experiments using TCRαβ and on cells displaying the full αβTCR holoreceptor (Das et al., 2015; Banik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is experimental observation from cited studies.

claim: Since Vαβ-pMHC lacking the C-module forms a more stable binding, the C-module likely undergoes partial unfolding in the extended state.
source: Since Vαβ-pMHC lacking the C-module forms a more stable binding (Figure 3) that was also observed in our previous simulations of the JM22 TCR (Hwang et al., 2020), the C-module likely undergoes partial unfolding in the extended state.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results and previous work.

claim: While the folded C-module serves as the base for the asymmetric V-C motion screening for the matching pMHC, once a match is found, the reversible transitioning propelled by the partial unfolding of the C-module may agitate the membrane and activate the cytoplasmic domains of the surrounding CD3 subunits to initiate downstream signaling.
source: Thus, while the folded C-module serves as the base for the asymmetric V-C motion screening for the matching pMHC, once a match is found, the reversible transitioning propelled by the partial unfolding of the C-module may agitate the membrane and activate the cytoplasmic domains of the surrounding CD3 subunits to initiate downstream signaling (Reinherz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for signaling initiation, combining simulation insights with cited work.

claim: A circumstantial evidence for the capacity of the C-module to unfold is that the Cα domain as well as parts of Cβ are occasionally unresolved in crystal structures, as in PDB 1AO7.
source: A circumstantial evidence for the capacity of the C-module to unfold is that the Cα domain as well as parts of Cβ are occasionally unresolved in crystal structures, as in PDB 1AO7.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures used as supporting evidence.

claim: Catch bond formation and subsequent reversible structural transitioning under applied load indicate that pMHC recognition requires energy input, for example from the actomyosin machinery.
source: Catch bond formation and subsequent reversible structural transitioning under applied load indicate that pMHC recognition requires energy input, for example from the actomyosin machinery.
evidence: This is an inference about the energetics of pMHC recognition.

claim: Wu et al., 2019 suggested a partial separation of the MHCα1-α2 peptide-binding platform from β2m with the attendant lengthening of pMHC contributing to a longer bond lifetime.
source: In addition to TCRαβ, MHC may also respond to load. Wu et al., 2019 suggested a partial separation of the MHCα1-α2 peptide-binding platform from β2m with the attendant lengthening of pMHC contributing to a longer bond lifetime.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Banik et al., 2021 observed a catch bond for CAR-pMHC, where just MHC is being pulled with an antibody.
source: Banik et al., 2021 observed a catch bond for CAR-pMHC, where just MHC is being pulled with an antibody.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: For T-cell-based cancer immunotherapy, mechanistic knowledge of the mechanosensing through a TCR has a greater practical significance.
source: Yet, for T-cell-based cancer immunotherapy, mechanistic knowledge of the mechanosensing through a TCR has a greater practical significance (Reinherz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the practical significance of the research, supported by citation.

claim: The force range tested by Pettmann et al., 2023 was up to 100 pN, where even systems exhibiting catch bond in the 10–20-pN range will switch to a slip bond behavior.
source: However, the force range tested was up to 100 pN, where even systems exhibiting catch bond in the 10–20-pN range will switch to a slip bond behavior.
evidence: This is a critique of the cited study based on knowledge of catch bond behavior.

claim: A catch bond exhibits a non-monotonic force versus bond lifetime profile, so that fitting with Bell's equation, an exponential function, leads to results that do not have a clear physical meaning.
source: A catch bond exhibits a non-monotonic force versus bond lifetime profile, so that fitting with Bell's equation, an exponential function, leads to results that do not have a clear physical meaning.
evidence: This is a critique based on knowledge of catch bond behavior and Bell's equation.

claim: The residues of the antigenic peptide play a role more as 'teeth of a key' for screening the TCRαβ-pMHC interaction fitness rather than bearing applied loads.
source: We earlier proposed that the residues of the antigenic peptide play a role more as 'teeth of a key' for screening the TCRαβ-pMHC interaction fitness rather than bearing applied loads (Hwang et al., 2020; Reinherz et al., 2023; Figure 1, 'bittings of a key').
evidence: This is a previously proposed model, supported by citations.

claim: The present study confirms the notion that peptide residues act as 'teeth of a key' through simulations of mutant systems.
source: The present study confirms this notion through simulations of mutant systems, where several contacts across the interface with pMHC were impaired due to a single-residue mutation on the peptide in ways that reflect the functional outcome of the mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutant simulation results.

claim: Stabilization of the inter- and intramolecular interfaces throughout the whole complex under 10–20-pN load would indicate a cognate TCRαβ-pMHC interaction.
source: Stabilization of the inter- and intramolecular interfaces throughout the whole complex under 10–20-pN load would indicate a cognate TCRαβ-pMHC interaction (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed criterion for identifying cognate interactions, based on simulation results.

claim: The features of stabilization under load are based on overall TCRαβ-pMHC complex dynamics, rather than changes to specific contacts or a particular conformational change, so they can be used to predict fitness of other TCRαβ-pMHC combinations.
source: Since these features are based on overall TCRαβ-pMHC complex dynamics, rather than changes to specific contacts or a particular conformational change, they can be used to predict fitness of other TCRαβ-pMHC combinations.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the findings.

claim: An in silico method would be needed that efficiently predicts dynamic properties of the complex based on sequence and structural data only.
source: Such tests involve performing many all-atom MD simulations and trajectory analyses. An in silico method would be needed that efficiently predicts dynamic properties of the complex based on sequence and structural data only.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Atomistic insights gained from the present study will be helpful for developing an efficient in silico prediction method in future studies.
source: Atomistic insights gained from the present study will be helpful for developing such a method in future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the current work.
